comments.text:
people living in ancient Greece and Rome also viewed old age as a distinct and inevitable stage of life, just as we do today. At some point, people entered a period of physical decline, and their roles within the community also changed. Although people were not aging at a tremendous speed, their concept of old age was actually different because the concept of "old age" is based on cultural norms.

Ancient Roman historians often emphasize the fact that there was no universally agreed-upon retirement age marking the beginning of a new phase of life. People generally considered themselves and others to be "growing old" when their appearance, physical strength, or mental acuity began to change. Because different people experienced a sliding scale of progressive physical and mental decline as they aged, whether a person of a certain age appeared old or was considered elderly varied depending on the circumstances. This was largely true during the Hellenistic period and in the Classical Mediterranean region as well.

Ancient writers generalized that the first signs of aging begin to appear at the time we today consider middle age and old age. Traditional signs of old age included hair loss, gray hair, wrinkles, deteriorating vision or hearing, arthritis, and weakness of the limbs. It was known that older adults were particularly more vulnerable to diseases such as respiratory illnesses. There was also a general loss of reproductive capacity in both sexes, represented by menopause in women and erectile dysfunction or infertility in men. Doctors generally attributed these changes to the body "cooling down" as it loses its natural heat over time.

These physical changes foreshadowed deeper shifts in lifestyle and behavior, determined by changing physical capabilities and social expectations. There was a perception that older people could not, and should not, act like young people. Modern historians have debated whether older people were respected or marginalized in ancient times. While aging was regarded as natural, depictions of old age in ancient art and literature often carry ageist nuances. Generally, there is a tension between norms that provide respect and support to wise and respected elders, and norms that ridicule them for being physically weak, less attractive, or foolish.

Greek writers traditionally divided human lifespan into distinct stages based not only on physical and mental abilities but also on social roles. Ptolemy, the astronomer of Alexandria, regarded the period from 56 to 68 as a time when men gradually retired from arduous labor and became more contemplative. From 68 onwards, it was a period of physical, mental, and social decline leading to death. Solon begins the final stage of human life at 63 but characterizes it using similar terminology. Other Greek writers make similar pronouncements regarding the stages of the ideal human life, but each stage begins at a different time. "Old age" may begin at 45 for some writers and 70 for others.

Since most of the literature that has survived from classical Greece and Rome focuses on the life experiences of male citizens, it is easiest to understand what aging meant to this demographic group. Although there was no universally agreed-upon standard date for youth, the general period during which male citizens in the ancient Mediterranean region were imagined to be aging was between 45 and 60 years of age. During this stage of life, men's social and political status often reached its peak, while their health was expected to decline. As men entered their 60s, they were increasingly perceived as typically "old."

While men's civic responsibilities and public status generally changed during this period, nothing approached a standard retirement age. In the Hellenistic Eastern Mediterranean region, it appears that elderly male citizens of the polis formed an age group distinct from the general citizenry (such associations of the elderly were generally called Gerousiae ). They can be likened to adolescents and young men. The exact age at which men could join the Gerousiae is unclear, but it was likely in their 50s.

In the Roman Republic and the Empire, men were freed from many state duties in their 50s and 60s and generally ceased participation in military or political life around this time. This inevitable withdrawal from civic life meant a loss of status as they moved away from the social roles associated with adult masculinity. However, it also meant they had the opportunity to enjoy greater leisure time.

For women, aging likely presented similar challenges. Menopause marked the end of a woman's reproductive life and served as a turning point for moving away from the socially expected roles of wife and mother. Since ancient writers generally placed menopause between the ages of 40 and 50, it appears this was the age at which women began to be regarded as old. Older women are more marginalized than older men in ancient sources, and there is relatively little evidence regarding how aging was imagined in women. However, regardless of gender, similar signs of age appear in depictions of the elderly. These include physical signs of aging (gray hair, wrinkles, etc.) and mental signs of aging (difficulties with memory and thinking).

As with men, whether a woman was "old" must have been determined by her appearance and ability. On the other hand, a woman's social status was inextricably linked to her husband, which meant they "aged together." Harlow and Laurence observed that because aristocratic women often married men about ten years their senior, they entered the social category of "old age" at a biological age lower than their husbands. The example of a 50-year-old woman and a 60-year-old husband illustrates this well.

Therefore, the point at which a man retired from public office at age 60 would often have coincided with the biological fact that his wife could no longer bear children. Her public role was intertwined with his perception, and the time she ceased pregnancy coincided with the time he could retire from office. In fact, Augustus's marriage laws created a course of men's political lives that aligned with the course of women's lives—marriage (and reproduction) with men of public age. [From "Looking at the Old: Recording and Honoring the Elders in Rome and the Empire" On Old Age ]

The experience of aging likely depended heavily on factors such as wealth and social status. For Ptolemy, the onset of old age was a man's "golden age," during which he spent his leisure and contemplation before true old age brought its bitterness and declining health. This was possible only for members of the landowning class who could retire and live off their own property and income from servants. In ancient Rome, an ideal vision of the leisure of old age is preserved in the literary works of aristocratic men in their old age who possessed the necessary resources, time, and education.

For most people living in ancient times, their livelihoods were earned through direct physical labor. Since there were no pension programs or welfare systems for the elderly, retirement was not always possible, nor was it an easy task. Lifelong inadequate nutrition and strenuous labor would have exacerbated the physical deterioration of aging, while the ability to perform physical labor would have been essential for functioning independently as an adult. It is highly likely that the poor were considered "old" at a relatively early age.

Growing Up and Growing Old in Ancient Rome by Mary Harlow and Ray Laurence

comments.text:
구석기시대 이전의 인간들도 사고사하지 않는 한 평균 70대 중반까지 살았다는 연구결과도 있죠.
그때와 조선시대의 차이는 단 두가지 뿐입니다.
첫째는 고대에는 수렵사회라서 육류 중심의 식단이었고 조선시대는 90% 이상 탄수화물만 먹고 살았죠. 탄수화물은 원래 동물이 먹고 사는 영양소가 아닙니다. 이세상에 탄수화물을 주식으로 먹는 동물은 수백만 종 중에 오직 인간밖에 없는데, 사실 인간도 원래는 탄수화물을 소화시키지 못하는데 80만 년 전쯤 진화의 영향으로 탄수화물 소화 효소가 생겨났죠. 우리가 잘 아는 아밀레이스. 그러나 못먹는걸 계속 욱여넣어서 억지로 소화가 가능만 해졌지, 못먹는 영양소죠. 개가 원래 늑대에서 파생되어져 나온 100% 육식 동물인데 개가 인간에게 사육되어지면서 신석기 농경사회인 약 7000년 전부터 개에게 아밀레이스가 급증하기 시작해서 현재는 개사료도 탄수화물이 주된 성분이죠. 그러나 여전히 개에게도 탄수화물은 독입니다. 오직 인간이 사육하는 개에서만 비만이 일어나죠. 
탄수화물은 몸을 구성하는 영양소가 아니라서 필수 탄수화물이 없고, 오직 잉여시에 지방으로 축적만 되는데, 쓰레기 지방만 쌓이죠. 호르몬을 만들고 각종 기능을 하는 지방은 탄수화물에서는 축적이 안되고 오로지 음식으로만 섭취할 수 있죠. 한마디로 탄수화물은 오직 에너지원과 살이 찌는 기능 두가지밖에 없습니다. 과거 식량이 부족할 때는 요긴하게 쓰였으나 현재는 육식이 충분히 가능하기에 쓰레기죠.
조선시대에 유독 창병이라고 불린 종기가 창궐한 이유도 탄수화물 위주 식단 때문에 몸에 염증이 심하게 많아져서죠.

두번째는 고대에는 많아도 20여명 모여 사는 정도의 소규모 사회였는데 조선시대는 마을, 도시마다 적게는 수백명에서 많게는 수십만 명까지 모여 살다보니 자연스레 감염 위험이 높아진거죠. 한 명만 감기에 걸려도 가족 전체에게 퍼지고 또 곱절로 불어나는 식으로 싹 퍼졌죠. 그 감기 바이러스가 조금만 돌연변이를 일으켜서 폐렴 바이러스가 퍼지면 그대로 역병이 돌아서 싹 죽어나갔죠.
